after: ## Why rocks, ores and minerals are finite
alt: Top: rock is replaced by the rock cycle over millions of years but extracted at tonnes per day, so use far outpaces replacement. Bottom: metal concentrated in ore is spread out by use into products, waste and landfill, where it is much harder to recover.
caption: Use is far faster than replacement, and used metal ends up spread out and hard to recover.

alt: Three columns. Reduce: use less, such as thinner cans, lighter car parts and longer-lasting goods. Reuse: use the object again without processing, such as reclaimed bricks, refillable bottles and repaired electronics. Recycle: process waste into raw material, such as melting cans, recovering copper and crushing concrete.
caption: Reuse keeps the object; recycling turns it back into raw material.

alt: Accessibility (nearby collection), ease (simple sorting and labelled bins) and education (knowing what, how and why) all lead to more material being recycled. Recycling reduces demand for new ore, usually saves energy and cuts landfill, but costs money and energy, struggles with mixed materials and contamination, and can only supply what is thrown away.
caption: Accessibility, ease and education decide how much is actually recycled.

alt: One benefit and one limitation for each of the seven strategies: reduce and reuse, recycling, efficient extraction, avoiding depletion, legislation, enforcement and alternative materials. For example, legislation applies to everyone but has no effect unless enforced.
caption: Every strategy has a benefit and a limitation; legislation needs enforcement to work.

alt: Three swaps: fibre-optic glass cables replace copper telecom cables, plastic pipes replace copper pipes, and recycled crushed concrete replaces newly quarried rock. Alternatives cut demand for scarce minerals and may be lighter or cheaper, but may themselves be finite or harmful, cost more or need new equipment.
caption: Swapping materials eases demand for scarce minerals, but the substitute has its own costs.

after: ## Worked example 1: how long will a reserve last?
alt: A graph of a 600 million tonne reserve. Extracting 20 million tonnes a year empties it in 30 years; if recycling and reduction meet a quarter of demand, extraction falls to 15 million tonnes a year and it lasts 40 years. The estimate assumes demand stays the same.
caption: Cutting extraction from 20 to 15 Mt a year stretches the reserve from 30 to 40 years.

after: ## Worked example 2: does making recycling easier work?
alt: Two bars out of 18,000 tonnes of metal waste. Before a kerbside scheme 4,500 tonnes (25%) were recycled; after it, 7,200 tonnes (40%). The mass recycled rose by 60%, but 60% of the metal is still not recycled, suggesting education is also needed.
caption: Recycling rose from 25% to 40%, a 60% increase in mass, but most metal is still not recycled.
